question.text: If insiders can systematically earn abnormal returns by trading on private, unpublished price-sensitive information (UPSI), which form of the Efficient Market Hypothesis is inconsistent with that outcome?

answer.text: Strong-form efficiency is supported, since insiders are the only group that can earn excess returns.
Weak-form efficiency is rejected, since insider trading is a technical-analysis phenomenon.
Strong-form efficiency is rejected — under strong form no investor group, including insiders, should be able to earn abnormal risk-adjusted returns.
Semi-strong efficiency cannot hold because earnings announcements are delayed.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per page 50, strong-form EMH holds that prices fully reflect all information — including insider/private information — and that no investor group should be able to earn above-average risk-adjusted returns. If insiders can earn abnormal returns by trading on UPSI, strong-form efficiency is inconsistent with that observation. Pages 548-551 describe the PIT obligations and controls that exist precisely because insider information is not impounded in prices. The Trap: Option A inverts the inference; under strong form, insiders should NOT earn abnormal returns. Option B mislabels insider trading as a technical-analysis phenomenon. Option D mis-identifies the form of EMH at issue. Note: The EMH form being tested is strong form, which uniquely covers private/insider information. Weak-form (past prices) and semi-strong (public information) are not the relevant filter.
